This calculator instantly converts tire size notation into the actual diameter and circumference of your tire.

intro: A tire size like **205/55 R16** hides the one number that actually matters when you change wheels: the **overall diameter**. Get it wrong and your speedometer lies, your odometer drifts, and the new tire may rub the bodywork. This calculator turns the three-part code into the real diameter, circumference, and revolutions per kilometer in one step.
keyTakeaway: Overall diameter = **(rim in inches × 25.4) + 2 × (width × aspect ÷ 100)**, in millimeters. When switching sizes, keep the new diameter within **±3%** of the original — beyond that, your speedometer reading and gearing change noticeably.

explanation:
## Reading the tire code

A size like **205/55 R16** packs three measurements:
- **205** — tread width in millimeters.
- **55** — aspect ratio: the sidewall height is 55% of the width (so 205 × 0.55 ≈ 113 mm of sidewall).
- **R16** — radial construction on a 16-inch rim.

Because the rim is given in inches and everything else in millimeters, you have to convert before you can add them up. That's exactly what trips people up.

## The formula, step by step

The sidewall sits on **both** the top and bottom of the rim, so it counts twice:

```
Diameter (mm) = (rim_inches × 25.4) + 2 × (width × aspect ÷ 100)
```

For 205/55 R16: (16 × 25.4) + 2 × (205 × 55 ÷ 100) = 406.4 + 225.5 = **631.9 mm** (~632 mm). Circumference is then π × diameter ≈ 1,985 mm, which sets how far the car travels per wheel revolution — the basis for speedometer and odometer readings.

## Why the ±3% rule exists

Your speedometer is calibrated to the factory tire's circumference. Fit a **larger** diameter and the wheel turns fewer times per kilometer, so the speedometer reads **slower than your true speed** (and the odometer under-counts). A **smaller** diameter does the opposite. Staying within ±3% keeps the error small enough that handling, gearing, ABS/traction calibration, and your speedometer all stay close to spec.

## Worked example: plus-sizing

Say the factory size is **195/65 R15** (≈635 mm) and you want 16-inch wheels. A **205/55 R16** comes out to ≈632 mm — only ~0.5% smaller, well inside ±3%, so it's a safe swap. Jumping to **205/60 R16** (≈652 mm) would be ~2.7% larger: still legal, but near the edge. Use this calculator to check any candidate before you buy.

For wheel fitment, load index, and speed rating, always confirm with your vehicle manufacturer or a certified tire professional.

faq.q: What does tire aspect ratio mean?
faq.a: Aspect ratio is the sidewall height as a percentage of tire width. A lower number (40%) means a flatter, sportier tire. A higher number (65%) means a taller sidewall with better comfort.
Rim diameter is the size of your wheel measured in inches. Common sizes are 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, and 20 inches. It's the third number in your tire size code (e.g., R16 = 16-inch rim).

faq.q: Can I use a different tire size?
faq.a: You can change tire sizes, but the new tire's overall diameter should be within 3% of the original. Larger deviations affect speedometer accuracy, fuel economy, and handling.

faq.q: How does tire size affect speedometer accuracy?
faq.a: Larger tires complete fewer rotations per mile, so your speedometer reads slower than you're actually going. Smaller tires have the opposite effect. Use this calculator to verify your speedometer accuracy.

faq.q: What's the difference between low-profile and high-profile tires?
faq.a: Low-profile tires have lower aspect ratios (under 50%), offering better handling and sportier feel. High-profile tires (over 60%) provide better comfort and smoother rides.
